BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION




IN THE MATTER OF SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC
SERVICE COMPANY'S APPLICATION FOR: (1)
REVISION OF ITS RETAIL RATES UNDER ADVICE
NOTICE 341; AND (2) OTHER ASSOCIATED
RELIEF
                                                Case No. 25-00079-UT

 SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY


                Applicant.




                     TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION

               TO THE COMPREHENSIVE STIPULATION

                                 OF

                             ED RILKOFF

           NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION

               ON BEHALF OF UTILITY DIVISION STAFF



                             July 7, 2026

Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff                   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1                                    I. INTRODUCTION

  2    Q.     Please state your name and position.

  3    A.     My name is Ed Rilkoff. I am Senior Policy Advisor in the Office of the Chief of

  4           Staff at the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission.

  5    Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony?

  6    A.     The purpose of my testimony is to explain Staff’s opposition to the Comprehensive

  7           Stipulation (“Stipulation”) filed in this case from an affordability and customer

  8           impact perspective. Staff does not oppose every individual provision of the

  9           Stipulation. However, Staff cannot support the Stipulation as a whole because the

 10           allocation outcome and resulting customer impacts are not fair, just, reasonable,

 11           balanced, or sufficiently supported.

 12           My testimony focuses primarily on jurisdictional allocation, class revenue

 13           allocation, rate design, and affordability. I rely on Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank for

 14           the technical support for Staff’s jurisdictional allocation, class revenue allocation,

 15           banding, and rate design recommendations.


 16         II. SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATION

 17    Q.     Please summarize your testimony and recommendation.

 18




                                                                                                        3
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1    A.      Staff opposes the Stipulation as filed. My testimony supports that position from an

  2           affordability and customer impact perspective because the Stipulation’s allocation

  3           outcome is not fair, just, reasonable, balanced, or sufficiently supported. In

  4           particular, the class revenue allocation imposes excessive increases on residential

  5           and small customer classes. While Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank’s cost-of-service

  6           and revenue allocation testimony supports increases for those classes, the

  7           Stipulation goes further and assigns increases of approximately 17.5% to those

  8           classes.

  9           I rely on Dr. Blank’s testimony for the technical support for Staff’s jurisdictional

 10           allocation, class revenue allocation, banding, and rate design recommendations. His

 11           testimony supports base rate increases of 10.11% for Residential Service, 12.49%

 12           for Residential Heating Service, 10.94% for Total Residential, and 12.23% for

 13           Small General Service. Those increases are meaningfully lower than the increases

 14           reflected in the Stipulation and, if adopted by the Commission, result in rates that

 15           are more fair, just, reasonable and affordable.

 16           For those reasons, from an affordability and customer impact perspective, I

 17           recommend that the Commission reject or modify the Stipulation as filed and rely

 18           on the allocation and rate design recommendations supported by Staff witness Dr.

 19           Larry Blank.

 20




                                                                                                     4
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1                       III. ANALYSIS OF THE STIPULATION

  2

  3    Q.     What is your primary concern with the Stipulation?

  4    A.     My primary concern is that the Stipulation places excessive, unfair and

  5           unreasonable increases on residential and small customer classes. The Stipulation

  6           provides for increases of approximately 17.5% for those classes. In my view, those

  7           increases are too high and are not adequately justified when compared with Staff’s

  8           filed evidence.

  9           By comparison, Staff witness Larry Blank’s testimony supports lower base rate

 10           increases for those classes. Dr. Blank’s testimony supports a 10.11% base rate

 11           increase for Residential Service, a 12.49% base rate increase for Residential

 12           Heating Service, a 10.94% base-rate increase for Total Residential, and a 12.23%

 13           base rate increase for Small General Service. Those increases are materially lower,

 14           more affordable and more reasonable than the approximately 17.5% increases

 15           reflected in the Stipulation.

 16           From an affordability and customer impact perspective, Dr. Blank’s testimony

 17           provides a more reasonable basis for resolving the allocation and rate design issues

 18           in this case.




                                                                                                     5
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1    Q.     Is Staff arguing that residential and small customer classes should receive no

  2           increase?

  3    A.     No. Staff is not arguing that residential or small customer classes should avoid rate

  4           increases. Staff recognizes that Dr. Blank’s cost-of-service and revenue allocation

  5           testimony supports fair, just and reasonable increases for those classes.

  6           Staff’s concern is that the Stipulation moves beyond Staff’s filed cost-of-service

  7           and revenue allocation position and imposes even higher increases on residential

  8           and small customer classes. In my view, that outcome is not reasonable, particularly

  9           given the affordability concerns facing households and small businesses.

 10    Q.     Why is the difference between Dr. Blank’s testimony and the Stipulation

 11           important?

 12    A.     The difference is important because Dr. Blank’s testimony provides an evidentiary

 13           basis for class revenue allocation, while the Stipulation reflects a negotiated

 14           outcome that is not sufficiently supported and increases the burden on residential

 15           and small customer classes beyond Staff’s filed recommendation.

 16           The difference is not minor. Under the Stipulation, Residential Service, Residential

 17           Heating Service, and Small General Service would receive base rate increases of

 18           approximately 17.5%. Under Dr. Blank’s testimony, Residential Service would

 19           receive a 10.11% base rate increase, Residential Heating Service would receive a

 20           12.49% base rate increase, Total Residential would receive a 10.94% base-rate




                                                                                                      6
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           increase, and Small General Service would receive a 12.23% base rate increase. Dr.

  2           Blank’s Table 2 also shows a Staff Total New Mexico Retail system average base

  3           rate increase of 6.65%, compared with 12.55% under the Stipulation.

  4           Figure 1 below compares the average bill impacts under Dr. Blank’s filed Staff

  5           recommendation with the average bill impacts reflected in the Stipulation.

  6

  7                             Figure 1. Average Bill Impact Comparison
               Customer Class                            Blank / Staff    Stipulation
               Residential                                  6.30%           13.60%
               Residential Heating                          6.90%           12.10%
               Small General                                7.50%           12.90%

               Secondary General                           16.60%           13.10%
               Primary General                              1.60%            6.60%
               LGS-T 69 kV                                 13.40%           18.30%

               Small Municipal & School                     4.10%           11.80%
               Large Municipal & School                     6.90%           14.70%
               Street Lighting                              5.20%           10.70%
               Area Lighting                               14.90%           20.40%

Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1

  2           This comparison matters because Dr. Blank’s recommendation is tied to Staff’s

  3           filed Direct cost-of-service and revenue allocation analysis. By contrast, the

  4           Stipulation produces higher increases for residential and small customer classes

  5           than Staff’s filed position, and those higher increases are not sufficiently supported.

  6           While settlements can involve compromise, a stipulation must still be reasonable

  7           and in the public interest.

  8    Q.     Does Staff’s opposition to the Stipulation also include the jurisdictional

  9           allocation issue addressed by Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank?

 10    A.      Yes. Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank sponsors Staff’s technical recommendation on

 11           jurisdictional allocation. My testimony does not sponsor the technical jurisdictional




                                                                                                        8
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           allocation calculations, but I support Dr. Blank’s testimony and recommendations

  2           from an affordability and customer impact perspective.

  3           Jurisdictional allocation matters because SPS is a multi-jurisdictional utility that

  4           allocates costs and benefits between New Mexico and Texas.            Jurisdictional

  5           allocation affects the overall revenue deficiency assigned to New Mexico retail

  6           customers. If New Mexico customers are assigned an excessive share of SPS’s

  7           system costs, that increases the amount that must be recovered through New

  8           Mexico retail rates. Dr. Blank’s Direct testimony estimates that his jurisdictional

  9           allocation recommendation would reduce SPS’s New Mexico revenue deficiency

 10           by approximately $56.7 million. That reduction is important from an affordability

 11           perspective because it reduces the overall pressure on all New Mexico customers’

 12           bills.

 13    Q.     Does Staff believe affordability should be considered in class revenue

 14           allocation?

 15    A.     Yes. My Direct testimony included an affordability framework and explained that

 16           affordability is broader than low-income assistance. It includes whether proposed

 17           bill impacts are reasonably absorbable for households and businesses and whether

 18           the costs driving those increases are fairly assigned among customer classes. In my

 19           Direct testimony, I also explained that affordability and cost causation should be




                                                                                                     9
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           considered together when evaluating whether rates are fair, just, reasonable, and in

  2           the public interest.

  3           Residential customers and small businesses generally have less ability to absorb

  4           large bill increases than larger commercial and industrial customers. Many

  5           households and small businesses must pay utility bills from existing monthly cash

  6           flow. A significant rate increase can require them to reduce spending on other

  7           necessary expenses.

  8           For that reason, the Commission should consider not only the total revenue

  9           requirement, but also how that increase is allocated among customer classes and

 10           whether the resulting increases are gradual, balanced, and reasonably absorbable.

 11    Q.     How does Dr. Blank’s testimony address affordability?

 12    A.     Dr. Blank’s testimony addresses affordability in several ways. First, Staff’s Direct

 13           testimony reduces the revenue deficiency from SPS’s proposed $175.4 million to

 14           $47.7 million. Second, Dr. Blank’s banding recommendation mitigates the

 15           increases to residential and small general service customers. Third, Staff generally

 16           supports the concept of an Electric Affordability Program, subject to Dr. Blank’s

 17           recommended modification. Fourth, Dr. Blank’s recommended rates produce

 18           average bill impacts of 6.3% for Residential customers and 6.9% for Residential

 19           Heating customers.     The Stipulation produces higher average bill impacts of




                                                                                                     10
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff   Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           13.60% and 12.10%, respectively, although those impacts are lower than SPS’s

  2           original proposal.

  3    Q.     Does Staff’s general support for an Electric Affordability Program change

  4           Staff’s opposition to the Stipulation?

  5    A.     No. Staff witness Larry Blank generally supports the concept of SPS’s proposed

  6           Electric Affordability Program, subject to his recommendation that the Percentage

  7           of Income Payment Plan initially be based on 5% of household income rather than

  8           SPS’s proposed 3%. Dr. Blank explains that the program is new, the benefit would

  9           be in addition to LIHEAP support, and the revenue impact on other customers is

 10           not yet known.

 11           However, targeted affordability assistance should not be treated as a substitute for

 12           reasonable jurisdictional allocation, class revenue allocation, and rate design. This

 13           is true because affordability assistance is targeted to a very small number of

 14           customers.   To affect large numbers of customers, even with an affordability

 15           program, the Commission must still determine whether the rates paid by all

 16           residential, small business, and other customer classes are fair, just, and reasonable.

 17    Q.     Is Staff asking the Commission to shield residential and small customer classes

 18           from cost-based increases?

 19    A.     No. Staff is not asking the Commission to shield any customer class from cost-

 20           based increases. Staff recognizes that Dr. Blank’s cost-of-service testimony




                                                                                                        11
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           supports fair, just and reasonable increases for residential and small customer

  2           classes.

  3           Staff’s concern is that the Stipulation goes beyond Staff’s filed cost-of-service

  4           position and assigns even higher increases to those classes. From an affordability

  5           and customer impact perspective, those higher stipulated increases are not

  6           adequately supported or reasonable when compared with Staff’s filed Direct

  7           testimony.

  8    Q.     Are you asking the Commission to adopt a separate alternative allocation

  9           proposal from Staff’s Direct testimony?

 10    A.     No. I am not presenting a separate alternative allocation proposal in this testimony.

 11           I am asking the Commission, from an affordability and customer impact

 12           perspective, to rely on Staff witness Larry Blank’s Direct jurisdictional allocation,

 13           class revenue allocation, banding, and rate design testimony.

 14           Dr. Blank’s Direct testimony provides the technical evidentiary foundation for

 15           Staff’s opposition to the Stipulation’s allocation and rate design outcomes.

 16    Q.     Why should the Commission rely on Dr. Blank’s testimony rather than the

 17           Stipulation?

 18    A.     The Commission should rely on Dr. Blank’s Direct testimony and testimony in

 19           Opposition to the Stipulation because it is based on Staff’s analysis of jurisdictional




                                                                                                        12
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           allocation, cost causation, class revenue allocation, gradualism, and affordability.

  2           It provides a record based, factual, transparent approach to determining the revenue

  3           deficiency assigned to New Mexico and allocating the approved revenue increase

  4           among customer classes.

  5           By contrast, the Stipulation produces higher increases for residential and small

  6           customer classes than Staff’s filed position which are not sufficiently supported.

  7           From an affordability and customer impact perspective, that outcome is not

  8           adequately justified, especially given the impact on those customers.

  9    Q.     Does Staff oppose the Stipulation simply because it differs from Staff’s filed

 10           testimony?

 11    A.     No. Staff recognizes that settlements often involve compromise and that a

 12           reasonable settlement may differ from any party’s litigation position.

 13           However, the Commission must still determine whether the settlement as a whole

 14           is reasonable and in the public interest. Here, Staff believes the class allocation and

 15           jurisdictional revenue deficiency allocation issues are significant enough that the

 16           stipulation should not be approved as filed. The Stipulation imposes approximately

 17           17.5% increases on residential and small customer classes, even though Staff’s

 18           cost-of-service and revenue allocation testimony supports lower increases and

 19           those classes generally have less ability to absorb large percentage increases than

 20           larger customers.




                                                                                                        13
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1    Q.     Is Staff recommending that the Commission reject every term of the

  2           Stipulation?

  3    A.     No. Staff is not saying that every term of the stipulation is unreasonable. Some

  4           provisions may be acceptable or may reflect reasonable compromise.

  5           However, jurisdictional allocation and class revenue allocation are central to the

  6           Stipulation. They determine the amount of revenue requirement assigned to New

  7           Mexico retail customers and how the approved revenue increase will be paid by

  8           different groups of customers. Because Staff believes the Stipulation’s allocation

  9           outcome is unreasonable, unfair and unjust, Staff cannot support the Stipulation as

 10           filed.


 11                                     IV. CONCLUSION

 12    Q.     What should the Commission do?

 13    A.     Staff recommends that the Commission decline to approve the Stipulation as filed.

 14           If the Commission approves a revenue increase, I recommend from an affordability

 15           and customer impact perspective that the Commission rely on the jurisdictional

 16           allocation, class revenue allocation, banding, and rate design recommendations

 17           supported by Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank’s Direct testimony and testimony in

 18           opposition to the Stipulation, rather than the allocation reflected in the Stipulation.




                                                                                                        14
Opposition Testimony of Ed Rilkoff    Case No. 25-00079-UT
   1           This approach would still allow reasonable, appropriate increases to be assigned to

  2           residential and small customer classes, but those increases would be lower than the

  3           approximately 17.5% base rate increases reflected in the Stipulation and would be

  4           supported by Staff’s filed cost-of-service evidence.

  5    Q.     Does this conclude your testimony?

  6    A.     Yes.
